I am seventy years old and have farmed these same 30 mu in Quzhou for fifty-five years. With six mouths to feed but some of my family working off-farm in the city, I cannot afford to take risks or chase fancy new methods. I have a good well, so when the rains fail I can still get water onto the fields. My wheat-maize rotation has never let me down, and this year I will stick to what I know.

It is early October, so I will start by preparing the land for winter wheat. I will run the rotary tiller over all 30 mu to break up the stubble left by the maize harvest and make a fine seedbed. Then I will sow my improved wheat variety at 40 jin per mu — I buy fresh seed every year because saved seed loses vigor. At sowing I will broadcast 100 jin per mu of compound fertilizer as a base, and come spring I will topdress with 60 jin per mu of urea when I see the wheat greening up. Wheat needs water at critical moments, so I will irrigate three times from my well: right after sowing to help germination, once before winter to protect against frost, and once at jointing when the tillers are forming. I will also spray twice for insects and once for weeds; the bugs and grasses here are stubborn. If the weather holds, I expect 1000 kg per mu.

As soon as the wheat is off the field in early June — usually around the sixth — I will plant denghai611 hybrid maize without any tillage. There is no time to waste between crops, and no-tillage has worked fine for me in recent years. I will put one package of seed per mu and apply 80 jin per mu of compound fertilizer at planting; that is enough to carry the maize through because the summer rains usually help. I will irrigate twice from the well if the dry spells stretch too long, and I will spray twice for insects and twice for weeds. I aim for 1000 kg per mu of maize too.

I do not change what works. My family depends on this land, and at my age I want steady, reliable harvests rather than experiments.
